title: Statistics Foundations: Data Types, Means & Outliers
description: Explore essential mathematical concepts through carefully crafted questions. Strengthen your understanding, practice your reasoning, and learn at your own pace.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a variable as categorical, discrete numerical, or continuous numerical.
questions.question: A survey records the brand of phone each student owns. What type of data is this?

options.label: A
options.text: categorical

options.label: B
options.text: numerical (discrete)

options.label: C
options.text: numerical (continuous)

questions.explanation: This data records categories or labels rather than numerical quantities, so it is categorical data.
questions.hint: Decide whether the data represents categories, counts, or measurements that can take any value in a range.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize how a truncated axis can create a misleading visual impression of a data comparison.
questions.question: A bar chart comparing two companies' annual revenue has its vertical axis starting at \(90\) instead of \(0\). Company X's bar looks twice as tall as Company Y's, even though Company X's revenue is only slightly higher. What statistical issue does this illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: The data itself must have been recorded incorrectly

options.label: B
options.text: Bar charts can never be used to compare two companies fairly

options.label: C
options.text: A truncated (non-zero) axis can visually exaggerate small differences between values

questions.explanation: Starting a bar chart's axis at a value other than zero distorts the visual proportions between bars, making a small actual difference appear much larger than it really is. This is a common way graphs can mislead viewers, even when the underlying numbers are accurate.
questions.hint: Think about how the starting point of the vertical axis affects the apparent height of the bars.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a data set.
questions.question: A set of video views (thousands) was recorded as \(90, 37, 69, 52\). What is the mean of this data set?
questions.explanation: Sum all the values: \(90 + 37 + 69 + 52 = 248\). Divide by the number of values, \(n=4\): \(\bar{x} = \frac{248}{4} = 62\).
questions.hint: Add all the values together, then divide by how many values there are: \(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n}\).

questions.learningObjective: Identify how an extreme outlier affects the mean compared to the median.
questions.question: A data set is \(20, 14, 26, 26, 13\). If an extreme outlier of \(180\) is added to the data set, what is the most likely effect on the mean and the median?

options.label: A
options.text: increases the mean, while the median changes very little

options.label: B
options.text: decreases the mean and the median equally

options.label: C
options.text: has no effect on the mean or the median

questions.explanation: Before adding the outlier, the mean is \(\bar{x} \approx 19.8\). After adding \(180\), the mean rises to about \(46.5\), since the mean is sensitive to extreme values. The median, which depends only on the middle-ranked value, shifts by at most one position and changes very little. Therefore, the outlier increases the mean, while the median changes very little.
questions.hint: The mean uses every value in its calculation, but the median only depends on the middle position.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a variable as categorical, discrete numerical, or continuous numerical.

options.label: A
options.text: categorical

options.label: B
options.text: numerical (continuous)

options.label: C
options.text: numerical (discrete)

questions.explanation: This data consists of countable whole-number values, so it is numerical and discrete.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a claim about a data set is mathematically consistent with a given mean.
questions.question: A data set has \(n=6\) values with a mean of \(20\). A student claims that all 6 values in the data set are greater than \(25\). Is this possible?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, this is always possible regardless of the mean

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, as long as the median is also greater than the mean

options.label: C
options.text: No, because the sum of the values would then exceed the total implied by the mean

questions.explanation: If the mean is \(20\) for \(n=6\) values, the total sum must be \(20 \times 6 = 120\). If every value were greater than \(25\), the sum would have to exceed \(150\), which is greater than \(120\). This is a contradiction, so it is impossible for all values to exceed the mean by that much.
questions.hint: Check whether the claim is consistent with the total sum implied by the mean: \(\text{sum} = \bar{x} \times n\).

questions.learningObjective: Select the most appropriate measure of central tendency for a given data scenario.
questions.question: A data set of shoe sizes sold in a store is being analyzed to determine which size to stock the most of. Which measure of central tendency is most useful?

options.label: A
options.text: mean

options.label: B
options.text: median

options.label: C
options.text: mode

questions.explanation: The mode identifies the most frequently occurring value, which directly answers which shoe size sells the most and should be stocked in the greatest quantity.

questions.question: A survey of 50 people asked their favorite color, with results: Red: 14; Blue: 10; Green: 11; Yellow: 15. What percentage of respondents chose Yellow, the most popular color? Round to one decimal place.

questions.question: A data set has \(n=6\) values with a mean of \(32\). A student claims that all 6 values in the data set are greater than \(37\). Is this possible?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: No, because the sum of the values would then exceed the total implied by the mean

questions.explanation: If the mean is \(32\) for \(n=6\) values, the total sum must be \(32 \times 6 = 192\).
